Work / Belmont Hill Club
BELMONT HILL CLUB · IDENTITY · APPAREL · SIGNAGE

A badge is not
a brand.

A racquet club mark, drawn as a donation to the club where I play. Years of apparel later, it needed the thing a logo never is on its own — a system.

Client

Belmont Hill Club, est. 1967

Services

Identity, palette, typography, apparel, signage

Marks

Badge · hawk · wordmark

Applied

Embroidery, screen print, headwear, signage

The finished hats and club tumblers. On the hat the hawk stands alone. The tumblers carry no other name, so they get the full badge.

The challenge

The badge was drawn in one pass, as a favor. Nobody asked what it would have to survive.

What it had to survive was everything: embroidered patches, screen-printed camp shirts by the hundred, visors, meshback caps, winter hats, tote bags, a road sign. Each ordered by a different person, from a different vendor, in a different year.

By the time anyone looked, three different color specifications were in circulation for the same two colors — PMS 583 and 295 in the master artwork, 383 and 281 on the headwear, 377 and 294 on the shirts. Six Pantone numbers for two colors. The vendors were not failing to match the green. They were matching a green nobody had reconciled.

The approach

Make one color the rule, not the fallback. Embroidery and screen printing both charge by the color. Specifying one-color navy removed the color everyone disagreed about and made the correct order the cheaper order at the same time.

Index by the object, not by the mark. “Which logo suits this application?” is a designer’s question and club staff cannot answer it. “What are you ordering?” they can always answer. The guide is a lookup table, not a menu.

Let the hawk off the leash. The badge had been doing every job, which is why every item looked like every other item. The hawk stands alone wherever the club name already appears on the piece — a rule that is checkable by looking at the object.

Artwork at 2.5 in. diameter, one-color navy for embroidery and stitch patch. The badge, the garment, and the number the vendor needs — on one sheet.

One color, by design

Every embroidered piece runs a single thread color — navy on light garments, white on dark. One thread, one setup, nothing to match, and it costs less than the version that goes wrong.

Headwear

Caps, visors and winter hats all run one thread color. The winter hat splits the identity across the cuff — the hawk on one side, the club name on the other. It reads differently depending on where you are standing, and because the name is still on the hat, the hawk is free to stand on its own.

Hawk 2 in. on the front, club name half an inch on the back, women’s and men’s identical. The hawk stands alone because the name is on the same hat.
The tote is the welcome gift for new members — usually the first piece of the club anyone owns, which makes it worth the two-color badge.

Off the court

The badge also has to behave on paper. Letterhead, envelope and card run the two-color version at small size against a single pea-green rule — enough club, not so much that a statement about unpaid dues arrives looking like merchandise.

Letterhead, envelope and business card, over an aerial of the grounds.

On the hill

At the Concord Avenue entrance the badge stops being a file and becomes an object — routed in relief, painted, and hung from an iron bracket. Most images on this page are mockups. This one is a photograph.

Carved in relief, which flattens the hawk into planes rather than lines. The mark survives the translation; the interior detail does not.

The outcome

The specifications converged. Current apparel runs on PMS 295 and 583 — the master colors — with one-color navy called out on the sheet the vendor actually reads. Alongside it: a three-page guide indexed by what you are ordering, an eight-color palette where every text color clears WCAG AA on the ground it is meant for, and a correctly-named file set including the one-color badge, which had never existed as its own file.

The mark did not change. What changed is that it can now be ordered correctly by someone who has never met a designer.
